content.text:
Part 1 — Answer

Short version: You can’t directly “prove” a person’s inner values, but you can test them against sustained choices, laws delivered, money moved, and political capital spent. Since taking office in December 2019, Ursula von der Leyen has repeatedly advanced, defended, and enforced human-rights protections through EU law, funding decisions, and foreign-policy instruments. The clearest evidence:

- Put enforceable rights at the core of landmark EU tech laws
  - AI Act: bans rights‑threatening AI uses (e.g., biometric categorisation by sensitive traits; untargeted scraping for facial-recognition databases; emotion recognition at work/schools) and regulates high‑risk systems to safeguard fundamental rights. Agreed in 2023, adopted in 2024–2025 by Parliament and Council. ([europarl.europa.eu](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20240308IPR19015/artificial-intelligence-act-meps-adopt-landmark-law?utm_source=openai))
  - Digital Services Act: the Commission’s own framework makes “protection of fundamental rights” a stated goal, giving users due‑process tools (explanations, appeals, data access) and imposing risk‑mitigation duties on very large platforms. Enforcement began 2023–2024. ([commission.europa.eu](https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age/digital-services-act_en?utm_source=openai))

- Built and used an EU “Magnitsky‑style” global human‑rights sanctions regime
  - The EU created a worldwide framework (Dec 2020) to target perpetrators of genocide, torture, arbitrary detention, etc.; it has since been renewed and expanded under her Commission. ([consilium.europa.eu](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2020/12/07/eu-adopts-a-global-human-rights-sanctions-regime/?utm_source=openai))

- Advanced women’s rights and anti‑violence protections
  - EU accession to the Istanbul Convention (entered into force for the EU on Oct 1, 2023) binds EU institutions to robust standards against violence toward women; von der Leyen publicly framed it as a values‑based step (“Europe is on the side of women”). ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/eu-accession-to-the-istanbul-convention.html?utm_source=openai))

- Required companies to respect human rights in supply chains
  - Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) adopted in 2024 obliges large companies to identify, prevent, and remedy human‑rights and environmental harms across their chains, with liability and penalties. ([consilium.europa.eu](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2024/05/24/corporate-sustainability-due-diligence-council-gives-its-final-approval/?utm_source=openai))

- Defended LGBTIQ people’s rights and the EU’s rule‑of‑law baseline
  - In her 2020 State of the Union address she condemned “LGBTIQ‑free zones” and pledged an EU “Union of Equality”; this was followed by an LGBTIQ Equality Strategy and concrete measures (e.g., denying certain EU grants to municipalities with discriminatory resolutions; Parliament later declared the EU an LGBTIQ Freedom Zone). ([enlargement.ec.europa.eu](https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/news/state-union-address-president-von-der-leyen-european-parliament-plenary-2020-09-16_en?utm_source=openai))
  - Backed rule‑of‑law conditionality: the EU suspended €6.3bn of cohesion funds for Hungary in 2022 over rule‑of‑law breaches; the Commission has maintained those measures pending genuine fixes. Using the budget to defend core rights is costly and politically hard, yet sustained. ([consilium.europa.eu](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2022/12/12/rule-of-law-conditionality-mechanism/?utm_source=openai))

- Backed accountability for atrocity crimes
  - The EU co‑launched the Atrocity Crimes Advisory Group for Ukraine and has coordinated support for international accountability, aligning EU policy with human‑rights law in wartime. ([eeas.europa.eu](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/ukraine-european-union-united-states-and-united-kingdom-establish-atrocity-crimes-advisory-group-aca_en?utm_source=openai))

What about counter‑evidence? There are credible criticisms that elements of the EU’s migration policy during her tenure — notably the EU–Tunisia deal and follow‑on steps — conflict with human‑rights safeguards (non‑refoulement, treatment of migrants, and civil‑society space). Leading NGOs have argued the arrangements risk EU complicity in abuses; several MEPs and media have echoed oversight concerns. These are serious and fair critiques. But they show a tension in one policy area more than they negate the overall, multi‑year pattern above: passing and enforcing rights‑centred EU law; conditioning EU money on rights and rule‑of‑law standards; and deploying EU foreign‑policy tools to protect rights. On balance, the evidence from law, funding, and diplomacy indicates she does value human rights, while some migration files remain contested and merit stricter conditionality and monitoring. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2023/07/eu-tunisia-agreement-on-migration-makes-eu-complicit-in-abuses-against-asylum-seekers-refugees-and-migrants/?utm_source=openai))


Part 2 — Sources I considered trustworthy (and why)

1) Council of the European Union (Consilium)
- Reasoning 1: Primary EU institution; official legal acts and decisions; high factual reliability.
- Reasoning 2: Used for AI Act adoption, Istanbul Convention accession, rule‑of‑law conditionality, and the Global HR Sanctions Regime — all first‑hand records of measures cited. ([consilium.europa.eu](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2024/05/21/artificial-intelligence-ai-act-council-gives-final-green-light-to-the-first-worldwide-rules-on-ai/?utm_source=openai))

2) European Commission (commission.europa.eu)
- Reasoning 1: Primary executive institution; authoritative on EU policy goals, enforcement, and implementation.
- Reasoning 2: Used for DSA purpose/rights features, the Commission’s stance on Istanbul Convention, and “Holding Russia accountable” — directly ties von der Leyen’s programme to rights protection. ([commission.europa.eu](https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/priorities-2019-2024/europe-fit-digital-age/digital-services-act_en?utm_source=openai))

3) European Parliament (europarl.europa.eu)
- Reasoning 1: Primary EU legislature; publishes votes, laws, and official news.
- Reasoning 2: Used for AI Act adoption and LGBTIQ Freedom Zone resolution; credible for tracing democratic mandates behind cited rights measures. ([europarl.europa.eu](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20240308IPR19015/artificial-intelligence-act-meps-adopt-landmark-law?utm_source=openai))

4) EUR‑Lex (eur-lex.europa.eu)
- Reasoning 1: Official EU law repository; definitive on legal status and entry‑into‑force.
- Reasoning 2: Used to confirm Istanbul Convention entry‑into‑force for the EU and CSDDD timelines. ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/eu-accession-to-the-istanbul-convention.html?utm_source=openai))

5) European External Action Service (eeas.europa.eu)
- Reasoning 1: Official EU diplomatic service; reliable for external human‑rights actions.
- Reasoning 2: Used for the Atrocity Crimes Advisory Group details and accountability support for Ukraine. ([eeas.europa.eu](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/eeas/ukraine-european-union-united-states-and-united-kingdom-establish-atrocity-crimes-advisory-group-aca_en?utm_source=openai))

6) EU Agency for Fundamental Rights (fra.europa.eu)
- Reasoning 1: Independent EU agency with recognised expertise on rights impacts.
- Reasoning 2: Used to explain DSA’s fundamental‑rights enforcement context; aligns with primary law and regulation. ([fra.europa.eu](https://fra.europa.eu/en/speech/2025/effects-digital-technologies-fundamental-rights?utm_source=openai))

7) Reuters
- Reasoning 1: Global wire service with strong editorial standards; fact‑checked, timely.
- Reasoning 2: Used for Parliament’s CSDDD vote and rule‑of‑law context updates; complements official acts with neutral reportage. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/eu-parliament-approves-new-business-supply-chain-audit-law-2024-04-24/?utm_source=openai))

8) Associated Press (AP)
- Reasoning 1: Highly reputable wire service; broad international coverage.
- Reasoning 2: Used for developments on the special tribunal initiative and Tunisia‑EU tensions; corroborates official narratives with independent reporting. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/4f0012e735e7968390a7eb2c0c331561?utm_source=openai))

9) Euronews
- Reasoning 1: Mainstream European outlet; generally accurate and balanced.
- Reasoning 2: Used for coverage of the Tunisia MoU and Commission conditionality debates; helpful context around official decisions. ([euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2023/07/16/tunisia-and-eu-sign-a-strategic-partnership-on-economy-and-migration?utm_source=openai))

10) Amnesty International
- Reasoning 1: Leading human‑rights NGO with rigorous documentation; widely cited by institutions.
- Reasoning 2: Used for substantive critiques of the EU–Tunisia migration deal and Tunisia’s crackdown; necessary to weigh counter‑evidence fairly. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2023/07/eu-tunisia-agreement-on-migration-makes-eu-complicit-in-abuses-against-asylum-seekers-refugees-and-migrants/?utm_source=openai))

11) Human Rights Watch
- Reasoning 1: Global NGO with established methodology; credible on rights conditions.
- Reasoning 2: Used for analysis arguing the EU under‑weighted rights in Tunisia; relevant to assessing limits of the claim. ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/05/12/eu-has-simply-abandoned-human-rights-tunisia?utm_source=openai))


Part 3 — Sources I considered not trustworthy for this task (and why)

- Wikipedia (topic pages consulted but not relied on)
  - Reasoning 1: Useful for orientation, but community‑edited and mutable; not a primary source.
  - Reasoning 2: For legal/policy claims (DSA/CSDDD), primary EU texts and institutions are stronger; I did not base conclusions on Wikipedia. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Services_Act?utm_source=openai))

- PinkNews, GMA News, eudebates.tv, UrduPoint, The European Times, Moneycontrol (articles encountered while scanning)
  - Reasoning 1: Mixture of advocacy outlets, regional aggregators, or low‑context reposts; standards and editorial controls vary.
  - Reasoning 2: Where official transcripts or major outlets were available, I avoided these for core claims; they were not necessary to substantiate EU legal acts or institutional positions. ([thepinknews.com](https://www.thepinknews.com/2020/09/16/poland-lgbt-free-zones-european-union-commission-president-ursula-von-der-leyen/?utm_source=openai))

- The Guardian (used sparingly)
  - Reasoning 1: A reputable newspaper but with a clear editorial line.
  - Reasoning 2: Cited only for reportage on political criticism (portfolio “downgrade,” migration‑deal scrutiny), not for establishing legal facts; primary EU records remain the basis of the proof. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/sep/24/equality-downgrade-european-commission-rights-groups-ursula-von-der-leyen?utm_source=openai))
